name: Blackbody radiation
seoDesc: Blackbody radiation: work out speed of light (c) from the peak spectral radiance and the exp var peak w. A free physics calculator with the formula, units…
summary: The Blackbody radiation calculator turns the peak spectral radiance, the exp var peak w and the spectral radiance into speed of light (c). That makes it useful for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Blackbody radiation calculator work?
sections.html:
The Blackbody radiation calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports speed of light (c) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case; then you type in the peak spectral radiance (Spectral radiance from wavelength), the exp var peak w, the spectral radiance (Spectral radiance from frequency) and the peak spectral radiance (Spectral radiance from wavenumber).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Blackbody radiation calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Speed of light (c)=(1 ÷ 2) × the square root of (2) × the square root of (exp var × spectral radiance × (wavelength of the radiation (λ) ^ 5) ÷ (emissivity of the body (ε) × planck constant (h)))
Speed of light (c)=boltzmann constant (k) × temperature of the body (T) × wavelength of the radiation (λ) × the natural log of (exp var + 1) ÷ planck constant (h)
Speed of light (c)=spectral radiance × wavelength of the radiation (λ) ÷ (planck constant (h) × photon spectral radiance)
Wavelength of the peak spectral radiance=(579554391 ÷ 200000000000) ÷ temperature of the body (T)
Speed of light (c)=(392069039487 ÷ 100000000000) × boltzmann constant (k) × peak wavelength of photon spectral radiance × temperature of the body (T) ÷ planck constant (h)
Speed of light (c)=(1 ÷ 2) × the square root of (2) × the square root of (exp var peak w × peak spectral radiance × (wavelength of the peak spectral radiance ^ 5) ÷ (emissivity of the body (ε) × planck constant (h)))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Temperature, opening in kelvins

  • Power, opening in watts

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Blackbody radiation calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the peak spectral radiance, the exp var peak w and the spectral radiance — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Blackbody radiation calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns speed of light (c), derived from the peak spectral radiance, the exp var peak w and the spectral radiance. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Blackbody radiation calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the peak spectral radiance, the exp var peak w and the spectral radiance, which is 11 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter temperature of the body (T) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Temperature of the body (T) opens in kelvins and the chip beside it offers 28 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Photon sigma stefan = 1520460859393136.5. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Blackbody radiation calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
